clue.text: Independent's last edition attracts love and goes quickly — can't believe it

indicators.note: the final letter of the word Independent is the one wanted here

parts.note: an issue is one edition of a newspaper or magazine
love is nil in tennis, written as the letter O
flies means hurries or goes quickly

explanation.surface: The Independent's final print edition draws affection and sells out fast, which readers find hard to credit.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue appeared as the Independent newspaper ended its print run in 2016, so the surface is topical.
explanation.definitionFit: Allusive definition: a whole fabric of untruths is something you simply cannot believe.

clue.text: Have a go, grabbing girl where skin is dressed

indicators.note: the attempt word holds the girl's name inside it, as if seizing her

parts.note: to have a go is to try
Anne is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Someone is told to make an attempt while seizing a girl in a place where people get dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: A tannery is a works where animal hides are dressed and turned into leather.

clue.text: Drew attention (lose no time!) to rat

indicators.note: the instruction in brackets tells us to drop letters from the word for drew attention

parts.note: something spotlit had attention drawn to it
no can be the letter O, a zero or nought

explanation.surface: Someone highlighted an informer, with a bracketed urging to hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: '(lose no time!)' reads as urgency but is the instruction: take O and T out of SPOTLIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang verbs for informing on accomplices to the police.

clue.text: Unleashes chaos to rock Sun

indicators.note: chaos implies disorder, so the following letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone lets loose disorder to shake up the Sun tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean releasing something pent up, like a cork popping from a bottle of fizz.

clue.text: See 1
Showing political unity in savage newspaper leader

indicators.note: the editor sits inside the word for savage

parts.note: feral means wild or savage
ED, short for editor, is the head of a newspaper

explanation.surface: A newspaper's chief writes a fierce editorial calling for political union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'newspaper leader' looks like a first-letter instruction, but it is the editor, ED.
explanation.definitionFit: A federal system unites separate states under one central government.

clue.text: It prevents rust in gold finish to exotic metal in heavy tap

indicators.note: gold comes as the finishing piece, placed at the end of the rest
the metal symbol goes inside the word for a blow

parts.note: a hit is a heavy blow or tap
Bi is the chemical symbol of bismuth, an unusual metal
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A recipe for a rustproof coating: gold over some rare metal, applied with a firm knock.
explanation.definitionFit: A corrosion inhibitor is a chemical that slows or stops a metal from rusting.

clue.text: End of quote from paper's other edition

indicators.note: the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A quotation's closing words are lifted from another version of the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of quote' looks like an instruction to take a last letter; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A defiant phrase tacked on at the close of a statement to say the speaker has had the final word.

clue.text: Guardian in conflict over retreat

indicators.note: in a down clue, over puts the first piece above the second

parts.note: war is armed conflict
a den is a private retreat

explanation.surface: The Guardian newspaper is caught up in a dispute about pulling back.
explanation.walkthrough: Guardian, capitalised, suggests the newspaper; it is just a keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: a warden is a keeper or custodian of a place or people.

clue.text: How the papers show the truth in ink, with balanced exchange of letters

definitions.text: How the papers show the truth

indicators.note: the letters are swapped around into a new order

explanation.surface: Newspapers present fact in print, setting out a fair correspondence between both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'balanced exchange of letters' sounds like fair correspondence on a letters page; 'exchange of letters' is the anagram signal, 'balanced' part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: something printed is set down in plain dark type on a pale page, as papers present facts.

clue.text: Crossword fan put off taking on Times

indicators.note: the discourage word takes in the multiplication sign

parts.note: to deter is to put off or discourage
the times sign in arithmetic is X

explanation.surface: A puzzle lover is discouraged from tackling the Times crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: Colin Dexter, author of the Inspector Morse novels, was a keen crossword solver and setter.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: the Morse novelist was famously devoted to cryptic puzzles, as is his detective.

clue.text: Consumer items for Boatman bound by a large number of perverse rules

indicators.note: the sailor is held inside the other pieces

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500

indicators.note: perverse means contrary, so the letters go awry

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor; Boatman is also this setter's name

explanation.surface: Goods meant for the setter are hemmed in by heaps of awkward regulations.
explanation.walkthrough: Boatman is the setter, so 'for Boatman' suggests 'me'; here it means a sailor, AB.
explanation.definitionFit: Consumer durables are household goods built to last, such as fridges and washing machines.

clue.text: Periods of confinement for deceitful offence

parts.note: lying means telling untruths, deceitful
a sin is a moral offence

explanation.surface: Prison terms handed out for dishonest crimes.
explanation.walkthrough: Confinement suggests jail; it is the old word for childbirth.
explanation.definitionFit: Old-fashioned term for the time a mother spends in bed around giving birth.

clue.text: Snapper we found misbehaving in one publication

indicators.note: behaving badly suggests letters out of their proper order

explanation.surface: A paparazzo is caught behaving badly by a magazine or paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily paper is one kind of periodical publication.

clue.text: One causes cuts in circulation, with red top in panic

parts.note: a lathe shapes material by cutting it while it spins round

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A tabloid with a red masthead causes sales to drop, sending the newsroom into a frenzy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'red top' suggests a tabloid, and 'circulation' newspaper sales; it is a turning machine plus R.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a lather is a state of nervous agitation, so the word means a fluster or panic.

clue.text: Bird in Mirror to mourn Independent, gutted

indicators.note: a mirror shows a word turned back to front

parts.note: to weep is to mourn

indicators.note: with its insides removed, only the first and last letters remain

explanation.surface: A bird in the Daily Mirror grieves for the closed Independent, which is left devastated.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mirror is a British tabloid newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the lapwing, a wading bird, is also named for its call.

clue.text: Former newspaper, one that never stopped

parts.note: ex means former
the press is the newspapers collectively

explanation.surface: A defunct paper is remembered as one that ran without a break.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Express is a British newspaper, but the definition is a fast train.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: a fast train runs through minor stations without halting.

clue.text: Article on Polish nudity

parts.note: the is the definite article
to buff is to polish

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about Polish people going naked.
explanation.walkthrough: Polish, capitalised, pretends to be the nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in the buff is to be naked, so the phrase stands for nakedness.

clue.text: Crooked act conceals class

indicators.note: the act word wraps around the class word, hiding it

parts.note: a deed is an act
a form is a school class

explanation.surface: A dishonest action hides its social status.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: both mean bent out of normal shape or misshapen.

clue.text: To the Left, Conservative way causes decay

indicators.note: reading leftwards means the following pieces are written backwards

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party
RD is the abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: A political observation: Tory policy, swung leftwards, leads to rot.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry rot is fungal decay of timber that crumbles wood in buildings.

clue.text: Here find a newspaper, a revered one; a river runs through it

indicators.note: the river name goes inside the newspaper's letters

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times
the Lee is a river in London and Ireland
ST is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A description of a London street of newspapers, a revered institution, with a river running beneath.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleet Street in London was the home of the British press and takes its name from the River Fleet, so the whole clue extends the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the London thoroughfare long housed the national newspapers, and still names that trade.

clue.text: "Goodbye Porkpie Hat" or "1,000 lost, sadly"?

indicators.note: in a sorry state, so the remaining letters are rearranged
the named letters are dropped from the hat words

parts.note: K stands for a thousand

explanation.surface: Two quoted titles: Mingus's jazz elegy for Lester Young, and a lament for a thousand dead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' looks like a link between the quotes, but its letters come out of PORKPIE HAT along with K, leaving PPIEHAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Allusive: an inscription on a tomb is a final farewell to the dead, as is Mingus's elegy.

clue.text: Fury at American church leader having cash injected by unknowns

indicators.note: the money letter is put into the church leader

parts.note: the Pope leads the Catholic Church
L, from the pound sign, stands for money
X and Y are unknowns in algebra

explanation.surface: Rage at a US prelate who has been slipped money by mystery donors.
explanation.definitionFit: A fit of apoplexy is extreme rage, as if anger brought on a stroke.

clue.text: Newspaper's leader has moral code about racial designation

indicators.note: the moral code goes round the newspaper's first letter

parts.note: an ethic is a set of moral principles

indicators.note: the leading letter of a word is its first

explanation.surface: An editor's column has principles regarding how race is labelled.
explanation.definitionFit: The word classifies people by shared cultural or racial origin.

clue.text: One's end: laugh wildly; guzzle an impala

indicators.note: the end of each of the following words gives a letter

explanation.surface: A scavenger's last moments: cackling crazily and gulping an antelope.
explanation.walkthrough: The rest of the clue also describes the animal, with its laughing cry and appetite for antelope.
explanation.definitionFit: Extended definition: the laughing scavenger of the African plains that feeds on antelope.

clue.text: Don't hinder telling of legend with face pulled repeatedly by hack, ok?

indicators.note: the word is spoken, so its sound is what counts

parts.note: a key or legend explains the symbols on a map
a pout is a sulky face
oft means often, repeatedly
to hew is to hack or chop
ay means yes, an agreement

explanation.surface: A grumpy-faced journalist is told to stop obstructing a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hack' looks like a journalist but means chop, HEW.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: staying clear of someone is the opposite of hindering them.

clue.text: Times, say, shows these unpaid workers absorbing a newspaper

indicators.note: the workers take in the newspaper letter

parts.note: serfs were feudal labourers working without wages
i is a British newspaper

explanation.surface: The Times reveals unpaid labourers taking in a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: Times New Roman is a typeface with small finishing strokes on its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the Times New Roman typeface displays small cross-strokes on its letter ends.

clue.text: Couple lose last scrap of hope in case

indicators.note: a letter is taken away from the case word

parts.note: an ...é case is a briefcase

indicators.note: the final letter of the word is the one taken

explanation.surface: A pair abandon all hope in a legal matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' looks legal; it is a briefcase.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: to couple is to join or fasten together.
